articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved an employment agreement appointing former City Administrator Paul Benoit as a retired annuitant to provide consulting services on the design and construction of a new community pool. Funding will be provided by Measure UU, a bond approved by voters on November 3, 2020. Benoit will be assisting current City Administrator Sara Lillevand on the project. The passage of Measure UU marks the first successful capital bond measure in the city’s history, Lillevand explained. Given the size and scope of the project (estimated at $19,000,000), she recommended at last night’s meeting. that city council add Benoit as a Special Assistant to this effort. “Paul is well known to the community, as he served as City Administrator from 2014-2019. During his time in this position, Paul shepherded the community process to develop the Aquatics Master Plan Conceptual Design, which was accepted by the City Council in 2016 and will be refined and implemented with the Measure UU funds,” Lillevand explained. “In addition to his familiarity with Piedmont and the Community Pool project, Paul has overseen large capital projects in Alameda, California and Astoria, Oregon,” she added. Benoit will be an invaluable addition to the internal city team, she added. His initial tasks will include leading the efforts to hire project management services, as well as the architectural design team. As a retired annuitant, the former city administrator can work a maximum of 960 hours in a fiscal year. Retired annuitants cannot be employed in any regular staff position. The maximum annual cost of the agreement is $106,000. These expenses are directly related to the construction of a new community pool, so Measure UU bond proceeds will be utilized, and there will be no adverse impact on the city’s general fund budget.

articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board convened for a meeting on January 13 with a discussion mainly on Governor Newsom’s “Safe Schools for All Plan.” The plan, if approved by legislators, would change the requirements for TK-5 classes to reopen and pay districts to have in-person classes. Piedmont Superintendent Randy Booker and the school board reviewed the implications and associated complications. School reopening remains just as cloudy, if not more so, than before. The plan, announced December 30, has received much criticism from school superintendents across the state. A main benefit of Newsom’s plan is an incentive of $2 billion to school districts that reopen. Districts that submit their application by February 1 and get approved would receive $450 per student, plus an additional amount up to $250 per low-income student. Piedmont would stand to receive $1 million in funding with this plan. Approved applications would let TK-2nd grade start February 15, and grades 3-5 on March 15. A later application deadline of March 1, for a March 15 opening, would give districts $337 per student. Another benefit is that the criteria for districts to reopen schools would change to an “adjusted value” of fewer than 25 new COVID-19 cases per day (per 100,000 population). This level (an unadjusted value of around 500 Alameda County cases per day) would have to be maintained for a five consecutive days. The previous red-tier requirement for reopening was 7 new cases per day per 100,000, and it needed to hold there for two weeks. On January 17, Alameda County’s case rate was 37.7. Newsom highlighted those positives to his plan but many superintendents and school boards across the state vehemently object to the newly imposed mandatory impediments to reopening. articles.text: The following article was written on March 7, one week before everything came to a screeching halt in Piedmont and throughout Alameda County. This article was first published in The New York Review of Books as part of its dispatches from around the world documenting the coronavirus outbreak. town San Francisco, already void of tourists, had turned ghostlier still. From behind the glass door of a shuttered Illy café on Battery Street, the Italian manager waved at me, his hand in a blue disposable glove, with an apologetic smile. For days, his parents, quarantined in Florence over the coronavirus epidemic, had been imploring him to stay away from people. It seemed as if they got their wish granted. weaving our way toward the Oakland maze. My neighbor’s parents had been on that ship; they were now at Travis Air Force Base, awaiting the results of their testing. I spent the weekend oscillating between “this can’t be real” and asking myself myriad odd questions, such as whether to explain to the kids, at least to the sixteenyear-old, how to claim our life insurance. I raided the rapidly depleting grocery aisles, picking up things I never thought I’d need, like pinto beans or soap in a 12-pack, all the while feeling the futility of the effort. If growing up in the shortage-ridden Soviet economy taught me anything, it’s that you can’t outsmart malfunctioning lines of supply and demand. We never knew what would disappear next, and even when we guessed right, the supply would eventually run out. The one thing that’s worth stockpiling is decency, that silver lining of our lives back in the USSR, with its near-permanent state of national emergency. Today, in America, where decency has taken a beating over the past four years, it might mean something as straightforward as not buying both of the last two loaves of bread, not forwarding that doomsday chain e-mail, and not going out even if you are healthy. Tomorrow, our challenges might not be so simple. Since I started writing this, a shelterin-place order for six Bay Area counties, including mine, has been issued. Decency won’t save us, but it will make our altered lives more tolerable, come what may. Anastasia Edek is a Piedmont writer author and lecturer. articles.text: This letter was sent to members of Piedmont City Council. Editor: I am a co-founder of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. I recently stepped down from the PCA Board to pursue other endeavors, but I served 9 years as program director, visual art program director, and juried art show administrator. As a board member and with no paid staff, I have put in countless hours at all hours of the day and night to help PCA grow into the City of Piedmont treasure that it is. The people of Piedmont love PCA. I have been thanked probably a thousand times by people who have attended events at the Center. Residents truly appreciate having an arts center as part the offerings of the City of the Piedmont. It ranks up there along with the school system and our well-run town. I have been told the PCA is one of the top 5 selling points of Piedmont cited by realtors. The Center for the Arts is now part of the fabric of this town. In this divided time, it is easy to allow a couple of disgruntled voices to overshadow all the good work that PCA has done in the last nine years. I have heard about false and unsubstantiated claims being made. I believe that the claims are being put forth for personal reasons or grudges. Other claims are for personal gain if PCA should be disbanded.
articles.title: PCA co-founder urges support by Council

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: I’d like to express my deep appreciation for everything the Piedmont Center for the Arts has done over the years for my organization, and for the supportive and welcoming way in which they foster our creative collaborations. I’m a founding member of the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV) and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) will co-host a virtual panel discussion on January 28, titled “Reimagining Public Safety: Can Surveillance be a Fair and Effective Tool?” The panel will include individuals in the public safety sector and is a follow-up to a similar panel discussion the League held in 2017. Panelists will include Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers; Brian Hofer, Chair of the Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission; Jennifer Jones, Technology and Civil Liberties Fellow at ACLU Northern California; and Mathew Guariglia, a Policy Analyst for Electronic Frontier Foundation. The discussion, via Zoom, is intended to focus on how surveillance impacts racial justice and public safety in Piedmont and the broader community. New surveillance technologies monitor, track, and predict the actions of citizens, and are becoming increasingly popular in public safety. The discussion will explore whether new technologies can help create unbiased, inexpensive public safety and justice, or if they are inherently problematic. Brian Hofer, Chair of City of Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission, will join a discussion panel on Public Safety co-hosted by the League of Women Voters and Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. articles.text: Oakland Congresswoman Barbara Lee Piedmont and East Bay residents gathered virtually for the City of Piedmont’s 24th annual Martin Luther King, Jr. Day celebration, held on Monday, January 18. The intersection of power, love and justice was the theme of this year’s event. Due to the ongoing health pandemic, the celebration, which usually draws hundreds to Piedmont’s Veterans Hall, was held virtually this year in observance of shelter-in-place regulations. Jodi Biskup, a moderator for the event, said that over 300 people registered via Eventbrite, making it one of the most well-attended MLK celebrations in Piedmont’s history, albeit virtually. The city historically draws a large crowd during this celebration, due in large part to the talent and broad reach of speakers and performers. This year was no different; featured speakers included Congresswoman Barbara Lee, California State Senator Nancy Skinner, Stanford Professor and King Institute Director Clayborne Carson, Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, and filmmaker and World Trust Founder Shakti Butler. Congresswoman Lee recalled the events of the January 6 domestic attack on the capitol in her observance of Martin Luther King, Jr. Day. “Racism is alive and well in America. Just two weeks ago, the U.S. Capitol was stormed in a violent attempted coup by white supremacists,” she said. “A confederate flag was brought into the Capitol, a noose was hung outside and Black Capitol Hill police officers – while defending our democracy, the Capitol building, members of Congress and staff – had to fight in combat to defend themselves.” Lee added that the murders of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and so many more at the hands of police officers, combined with the disproportionate impact of COVID-19 on people of color, prove that inequities in our country continue. “Dr. King passed the baton to us and gave us his marching orders,” she said. These events also host unique, local talent, especially from East Bay youth. This year featured traditional Native America flutist Vince Rehouse and Destiny Arts Youth Performance Company. The event closed at 12:30 p.m. with a brief video of late U.S Representative John Lewis, a champion of the Civil Rights era. King Institute Director Clayborne Carson A wide range of non-profit organizations and other groups hosted well-attended workshops following this year’s virtual event, a first for any Piedmont Martin Luther King, Jr. celebration. The Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) presented a book club discussion on the New York Times podcast “Nice White Parents,” hosted by Serial reporter Chana Joffe-Walt. The podcast focuses on a middle and high school that was formerly known as the School for International Studies (SIS) in Brooklyn’s gentrified Cobble Hill neighborhood. Participants discussed whether there were found parallels between Piedmont Schools and SIS. The Piedmont for Oakland Public Schools (POPS) hosted a discussion on the broader picture, and whether segregation is still alive in school across the United States education system. The organization supplemented the event with excerpts from Coretta Scott King. Piedmont youth were also involved in the virtual celebration. Piedmont High and Middle School’s Black Student Union (BSU) shared a brief video in which students addressed current events, and PHS 2009 graduate Aksumawi Turner hosted a podcast entitled “Perspectives on Power and Love: An MLK Roundtable.” For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Daniel Gonzales began his first day as Piedmont’s Public Works Director on Monday, January 11, and the beginning of his second week on the job proved eventful. High winds throughout the Bay Area toppled trees in Piedmont and created some damage. “We did have a few downed trees, including one on Oakland Avenue,” Gonzales confirmed. Fortunately, he added, the city’s Public Works crews already “knew the routine” and got in touch with PG&E quickly. There was no major damage, but crews were still hard at work clearing debris and monitoring strong winds yesterday afternoon. “Any time you have wind at that velocity, there’s a chance that it will wreak havoc,” he said. That is just a small sample of the scope of integral services Public Works provides. While Gonzales will be tasked with leading the department through large, ongoing projects, there is always work to be done “behindthe-scenes.” Piedmont’s Public Works Department oversees all maintenance to city infrastructure services, and the director is expected to guide the department through these major and minor tasks. Gonzales said one of his first priorities in the new position was getting to know his field staff. “Day one was getting set up and just getting oriented,” he said. “But for me, getting to know staff right away is a priority. [They] want to put a face to the name, and [I wanted to] have some interaction with them so they know what to expect.” Much of the support work in the department is conducted virpanel of city staff and residents. The interview process was virtual. Final candidates were interviewed on November 6, 2020, and the City Council formally announced on December 21 that Gonzales would be the department’s new director. Gonzales recognized the high expectations placed on him because of the efficacy of his two predecessors, Nakahara and Larry Rosenberg. “[Nakahara] had been in Piedmont for a quite a long time and certainly left his mark, not just on the department, but on the entire community,” Gonzales said. “That’s a tough act to follow, and you hope that you will be able to carry on that legacy.” Gonzales added that he is looking forward to connecting with the Piedmont community at large and “continue [Nakahara’s] relationship” with Piedmonters. In terms of demographics, it’s very similar,” he said. “There’s also an expectation of a high level of service, that I prided myself on providing to the residents there. I expect to provide that level of service to Piedmont.” Gonzales also worked as a Senior Engineer with CSG Consultants in Foster City, and has Daniel Gonzales tually, just as most city departments have been conducting business virtually due to shelterin-place regulations. Department head meetings are all remote at this point, which means new hires are not able to meet city staff the way they normally would. articles.text: Nate Redinbo The City of Piedmont is currently considering the adoption of Reach Codes to help the City meet Climate Action goals set by the City Council. Natural gas emissions from residential homes are one of the leading causes of greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont, and the proposed reach codes will reduce natural gas emissions. On July 20, 2020, the Council considered a package of proposed local amendments to the California Electrical Code, Residential Code, and Building Energy Efficiency Standards. The amendments – collectively referred to as “Reach Codes” – would alter the requirements for home construction and renovation in Piedmont to facilitate building insulation, electrification, and solar panel installation. Council approved the first reading of the proposed codes and directed staff to conduct additional research and public engagement leading up to a second reading. Part of those engagement efforts included a random sample representative survey of Piedmont registered voters on the proposed codes. In November and December 2020, the research firm FM3 conducted an additional city-wide voter survey to supplement the public opinion survey that was completed in June 2020. The latest survey asked 384 Pied- • mont residents their opinions on the proposed reach codes and how the codes would affect them. On January 19, City Staff and FM3 researchers will present the results and analysis of this survey to the City Council. Here are some of the key takeaways from the survey: • Most residents are concerned about climate change, with nine in ten saying that climate change will harm future generations. Seven in ten say that climate change is a serious problem and immediate action is necessary. • Of those familiar with the City’s Climate Action Plan, half say that meeting the plan’s objectives is very or extremely important. • Two thirds (66%) of Piedmont voters say they support revising building codes to reduce natural gas in city buildings. This percentage has remained consistent between the two surveys that have been conducted (66% supported this proposal in June). • Three in four say the most convincing reason to support adopting the Reach Codes is the impact of greenhouse gas emissions reductions generated by homes. When presented messages opposing the Reach Codes: 87% are concerned about being vulnerable during power outages; 81% are concerned that the proposed reach codes are unfair to those who have already taken energy efficiency actions; and 79% of residents are concerned about costs related to renovations. Staff has worked to address these concerns in resources on the City’s website, as well as in the staff reports to City Council. To learn more about exceptions to the solar panel requirements, what the proposed reach codes include, and expected costs of the upgrades, please visit the reach codes webpage at https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city _news_ _ _notif ications/ reach_codes. Unless otherwise directed by City Council, City staff intends to bring forward a second reading of the Reach Codes at the February 1st City Council meeting. Alyssa Dykman is a Sustainability Program Manager for the City, and Nate Redinbo is Piedmont’s Civic Spark Fellow.

articles.text: Piedmont school psychologists Kate Nolda and Alejandra Ojeda-Beck provided some additional information about the controversial mental health screener sent to all students on September 30. Nolda and Ojeda-Beck helped clarify the timing of reporting the results, specific findings and what has been done in response. Two weeks ago the Post wrote a story on results from the vague presentation to the school board on the screener. Last week parents weighed in on the survey and provided their tales of student struggles. A big concern of parents was the delay in reporting the results of the survey. Some felt that the delay in publishing results rendered the survey itself meaningless; everything in students’ lives had changed between September and December, when results were made public., Beck-Ojeda, the school psychologist at Beach Elementary School, explained, “The screener went live September 30 and stayed open for a little more than two weeks. Then we actually were able to close it and remove names for privacy, then get it over to Cal the same day for a professor and graduate student in psychology to ‘norm the results’ [rank them against other Piedmont students].They returned it to us November 5.” From there the results went to each school site on November 16, one month from the survey closing. However, Nolda and Beck-Ojeda had been sharing the results of the survey with counselors, teachers and staff since October. “People working directly with kids had working information very quickly. It took a while however, to get it into the hands of the board, district administrators and parents clubs,” Beck-Ojeda said. Many parents have contacted the Post about the screener and want to know what is being done about the results, which show high levels of student stress and mental struggle. “Our first step was to ID the students that were already connected with a resource [a counselor or the wellness center]. Then we looked at students who were not previously on our radar and we started tying them to resources we have.” Nolda said. “At Beach, I don’t think it is a secret that our kids are struggling. I think the teachers are hearing that and I think the school staff is hearing it. Even if the kids aren’t receiving one-on-one counseling, that doesn’t mean they aren’t receiving some kind of support,” she said. Both school psychologists praised the work of the teachers and mentioned a few exceptional teachers by name, two of whom are quoted below. “I’m making moves this semester to ‘go gradeless,’ a systemic approach to providing comment-only feedback throughout the semester that should hopefully address student anxiety and depression,” said PHS English Teacher Aaron Barlin. “I am offering small group discussions, games, validating their fears and hopes, and just allowing them to laugh with each other,” said Lesley Wighton, a 4th grade teacher at Beach. “I also remind my students how they can be helpful to their families. They are an exceptional group of students who are showing empathy and perseverance.” All of this may merely amount to damage control, however. At the latest school board meeting on January 13, the prospect of school reopening was less than definitive. This prompted frustrated board member to shift their focus towards the mental health of students right now. “In some way, through parent clubs or student clubs, we need to safely have face-toface interactions between students to address social emotional health,” board member Amal Smith urged. Nolda unraveled some of the results from the screen from her site at Piedmont Middle School. “More of our 6th graders are feeling school connectedness than 8th graders, one reason is developmental, in 8th grade peer connection is more important. Another part of it is the structure, in 6th grade students have a core teacher that teaches multiple periods, but in 8th grade they have different teachers for every single class,” she said. Beck-Ojeda reported on the elementary level. “We had very high levels of externalizing [aggression, hyper-activity, attention problems, and acting out] across all 3 schools. Their responses were between ‘often’ and ‘almost always’ [the two highest possible answers].” The screener was not perfect, but tons of work went into it, starting in April last year by a team of 18 people, including district counselors, psychologists, and staff members. “This was our first attempt at doing something like this. There may be things we will shift moving forward depending on our reflection of how this rolled out,” Nolda said. “It is an ongoing conversation. There is nothing set in stone. All of this is to best help our kids. If there is a better way to do it, we are incredibly open to it,” Beck-Ojeda said.

articles.text: The fragmented remains of the Fasti Praenestini of Verrius Flaccus, a Roman calendar from around the years 6-8 BCE. Happy New Year from all of us at Chabot. At the beginning of the month, we launched into a new year with new curiosities to explore. Most nations around the world celebrate a common New Year’s Day on January 1st, even those with different traditional dates for the starting day of their cultural new year. But Why January 1? The answer dates back about 2000 years to the days of the Roman Empire. Originally, the Roman calendar had 10 months that contained 304 days and began on the Vernal Equinox, the first day of Spring. The ancient Romans seem to have ignored the remaining 61 days, which all fell in the wintertime anyway and weren’t that useful to agriculture and sport. Those ten months were named Martius, Aprilis, Maius, Junius, Quintilis, Sextilis, September, October, November, and December. Those last six names literally mean the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth months. Staying in synch with the seasons Eventually, the Roman king Pompilius added January and February to the calendar, making it 355 days long. To make up for the ten-day shortage and keep the calendar in sync with the seasons, a short month, called Mercedinus, was added every two years, immediately following February – the same spot we tack on an extra day every four years on leap year to do the same thing. The new Julian Calendar The adjustment still wasn’t perfect, and over the centuries the year got out of sync with the seasons again. So, around 46 BC, Julius Caesar did something remarkable: he asked the scientists what to do. He consulted the best astronomers and mathematicians, resulting in the new Julian calendar – as well as a name change for the month Quintilis, which became July, for Julius. Later on, Augustus Caesar made his own mark with a name change for Sextilis: August. Julius Caesar declared January 1 as the first day of the new Julian calendar year – an appropriate choice, since January is named for Janus, the god of beginnings, transitions, time, passages, and endings. Ben Burress is an astronomer at Chabot Space and Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. But you can check out the Virtual Balloon Drop New Year Celebration at https://chabotspace.org/ events/events-listing/

articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Cynthia Kane is offering a new course through the Adult School designed for grandparents of all ages. Gather virtually with other grandparents to explore how it feels to have a new baby in the family, and to navigate the joys and challenges of a role that’s completely new to you, yet remarkably familiar. What has changed and what hasn’t in the world of childrearing/ How does the pandemic affect your experience and your family’s daily routine? We will review current child health and safety recommendations and have time to share grandparenting experiences in a safe and confidential space. The course is online and is scheduled for two sessions, with four classes each. Session 1: Saturdays, January 23 to February 13; 11:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Session 2: Saturdays, February 27 to March 20, same time. The fee is $60 per session. To register, see: https://piedmontadultschool.asapconnected. com/#CourseID=238892. Instructor Bio Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. She has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership, and now works exclusively with grandparents and their families. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, education, and support for grandparents, particularly those providing care for grandchildren. Her website, https://itstheirturn. com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents.

articles.text: On January 6th, a day when Congress was certifying the results of the presidential elections, Trump supporters who believed the election had been stolen staged an insurrection in Washington, DC. They ransacked the Capitol, endangering legislators and others in the building. Most of the outnumbered Capitol police officers actually did their job and tried to keep the lawmakers safe and deserve the nation’s thanks. But those that were on the side of the rioters must be investigated along with the insurrectionists who defaced the Capitol and democracy itself. What happened in January was a stain on the country. Unless those guilty face proper consequences, this can happen again. That day I got a notification from a friend with news I didn’t want to believe. The Capitol building had been attacked. It shocked me so much that I sat in my room in disbelief for some time. My mother was crying in another room, so I went to comfort her. I messaged my friend, and we kept telling each other that it would be OK, and that we couldn’t wait until the destructive Trump administration would be out of the White House. During the remaining classes that day, I tried my best to not check the news live streams or the New York Times page every five minutes for new updates. Why wasn’t help coming for the people in the besieged Capitol? It was much later in the day when reinforcements arrived in D.C. I will always remember January 6th as the day democracy almost fell. I hope others will remember it as well. I recently found a phrase that is worth remembering: “As long as you aren’t hurting anyone, do what you want.” That seemed to be something shared by Republicans in congress. But I ask the Republicans who fanned the flames with rumors of a fraudulent election, was it worth it? Was it worth it to make the congressmen and women fear for their lives, that they might die at the hands of the people that they are trying to help? If you believe that the new President isn’t right for the country and you are ready to overthrow a democratically elected government just because you like your candidate more, I think you are on the wrong side of history. We see moving vans with boxes being moved out of the White House. The Trump administration is leaving. We saw the image of a person leaving the White House with the bust of Abraham Lincoln, “Honest Abe,” as he was known. It struck me as ironic. The bust was one of the pieces of art that Trump chose to have in the White House during his presidency, and now it has to go back to the museum. As Washington D.C prepares for the transition of power, they are on a tight schedule since Trump refused to concede. There will be just five hours to prepare for the Bidens moving in. With the large number of National Guard troops at the Capitol and White House – some say as many as 25,000 – the Capitol doesn’t look like it’s about to hand over power to an elected president. It looks more like it’s getting ready for a war. To those that participated in or encouraged the insurrection, I ask again: was all of it worth it? A peaceful transition of power should have been respectful and safe, not dangerous. comes out, Joe Biden will have been sworn in as President of the United States. articles.text: One of the Post’s best paperboys, Paul Clifford, is headed to a private high school outside of San Diego. His new school, The Army and Navy Academy in Carlsbad, will have in-person classes with limited class size. “There are a lot of opportunities for me to pursue and the structure of classes should be a lot better for me. Part of why I want to go back to in-person school is I learn better from one-on-one with teachers and working in groups with other students,” said Clifford. A passionate bicyclist and mountain biker, Clifford said he was able to deliver all the papers on his route every week in less than one hour. But his favorite part of delivering the papers was getting to know some of the residents. The future looks bright for Clifford, who wants to get a pilot’s license at his new school. He is also hoping to join the football team at Army and Navy Academy. “I am most excited about being right on the beach and being able to get into the water on the weekends to go swimming or boogie boarding. That will be pretty awesome,” he said Clifford is also an active Boy Scout, and currently is quartermaster of Troop 4. His goal is to attain the rank of Eagle. He said that he will be able stay active with Troop 4 by attending their meetings online. Piedmont Post paperboy Paul Clifford is heading to Carlsbad to attend the Army and Navy Academy, a private high school near San Diego.
articles.title: Paperboy Paul Clifford heading to Army & Navy Academy

articles.text: As coronavirus vaccines by Pfizer, Moderna, and Astrazeneca slowly roll out across the globe, scientists will learn more about vaccination efficacy. For now, even those that have received the vaccine need to continue to wear a mask and stay home. While vaccines are shown to prevent serious sickness and symptoms, it is too early to know if a vaccinated person can still spread the virus. Asking for an explanation the Post turned to Jeff Jones, a retired epidemiologist, and Piedmont High School science teacher John Savage. “Because the vaccines were built and tested for efficacy so quickly (in this case, the ability to prevent illness), there hasn’t been time to determine whether or how effectively vaccinated people might spread the disease, even when they personally don’t get sick,” said Jones, who holds graduate degrees in Epidemiology and Industrial Hygiene from the University of Michigan. Savage, Piedmont High’s Immunology and Physiology teacher explained some of the basic science on how a vaccinated person could still spread the virus. “Antibodies attack infecting particles. IgA antibodies (immunoglobulin A) are found in your nose and mucosal membranes. We know that an infection from Covid elicits a strong IgA [nose] response,” Savage said. “We know that vaccines typically elicit a strong IgG (immuWilliam Wyatt, an environmental services worker at UCSF, receives the first COVID-19 vaccine from fourth year school of Pharmacy student Matthew Aludino. noglobulin G) response which is found everywhere in the body.” explained Savage. The vaccine boosts your entire immune system by making an antibody that will be spread throughout your body. However, SAR-CoV-2 reproduces rapidly in the throat and nose. In a December NY Times article www.nytimes.com/2020/12/08 /health/covid-vaccine-mask. html, author Apoorva Mandavilli noted, “Some of those antibodies [IgG, everywhere] will circulate in the blood to the nasal mucosa and stand guard there, but it’s not clear how much of the antibody pool can be mobilized, or how quickly. If the answer is not much, then viruses could bloom in the nose — and be sneezed or breathed out to infect others.” A vaccine’s efficacy is measure by its ability to : 1) prevent infection and transmission 2) prevent disease 3) prevent severe disease. The Pfizer and Moderna vaccines are very good (95 percent) at preventing disease and severe disease. “For the vaccine to be sterilizing (prevent infection and transmission), we want it to reduce viral load in the nose and throat [IgA],” Savage said. In addition to keeping others safe, patience is crucial after getting the vaccine. “It takes 4-6 weeks for vaccines to fully stimulate immunity, so you can still get sick during that period.” Jones explained. Piedmonters are encouraged to get vaccinated for personal safety, but to continue wearing a mask for the safety of others around you. for updates. Phase 1C includes those aged 50 to 64 as well as people aged 16 to 64 with underlying health conditions. People working in sectors like defense, energy, communications, finance, and government operations are also in this phase. The state estimates that vaccines will be available to people in Phase 1C sometime in the spring. The state believes that the vaccine will be widely available to the general public beyond these specific groups by the summer or fall, although health officials noted that the timeline is subject to change. As of January 14, Alameda County has administered 83,350 doses of vaccine. Roughly half of these doses were manufactured by Pfizer and the other half were created by Moderna. These vaccines were granted emergency use authorization by the Food and Drug Administration late last year. Importantly, both vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. Doses of the vaccines are free in California. Statewide, 1,350,000 doses have been administered out of a current stock of 3.2 million doses as of this week. Compared to other states, California still lags in terms of vaccine distribution even though it possesses more doses than any other state.

articles.text: CDC guidelines should still be observed Epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford. Internationally renowned epidemiologist and Piedmont resident Dr. George Rutherford joined the League of Women Voters of Piedmont for another virtual forum on January 13. The forum, “Are We Closer to the End?,” offered a hopeful look into the future as Piedmont, and the country, continue to weather this public health crisis. Staff Photos The Old Tree, estimated to be 1,200 years old, 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter, is at the end of the Old Tree Trail in Portola Redwoods State Park near La Honda in San Mateo County. Hikers can see the burn marks from fires decades ago among the many first- and second-generation redwoods in Portola Redwoods State Park. and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks from generations ago still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found in the park. Aside from its awe-inspiring enormity, the 1200-year-old tree is among the few old growth redwoods to survive the lumbering that flourished in the 1800s. Returning to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill for about two miles with an elevation gain of 550 feet. As it intersects with the Slate Creek Trail, turn left to start the trail back to your car. Intersecting with Peters Creek, turn right and begin a 1.5-mile hike to a historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and ascending 500 feet to the end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than 6 feet, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. If you turn left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until coming to a T intersection. Turning right takes you to Upper Escape Road. Turning right again will allow a brief glimpse of Peters Creek on the trip back to the car, making it a 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. It’s worth noting that we crossed 18 hikers on the popular 0.6-mile out-and-back Old Tree Trail. Those numbers will increase Another downed giant in Portola Redwood State Park. when the campgrounds are open given its popularity for young families. Aside from towering redwoods in every direction, you can often spot chickadees chirping about, an occasional banana slug wriggling beneath you, and the woodpeckers knocking off in the distance. Coyote Ridge and Pomponio trails are closed due to the wildfires. The Iverson Trail on the way to Tiptoe Falls is also closed. However, the brief walk to the Pascadero Creek is open. Cross-country has been given the okay to compete in the Purple Tier, but is waiting for Alameda County’s stay-at-home orders to be lifted. NCS Commissioner Pat Cruickshank explained in a recent press release that the Section’s current schedule will be finalized by January 29. “With input from our member schools and League Commissioners, the Executive Committee took action today to move forward with our calendar by giving leagues the autonomy to build their season of sport calendars around the guidance from the California Department of Public Health, the local counties that their league resides in, and the approval of their member schools and districts. This action will be subject to approval by the Board of Managers at their January 29, 2021 meeting,” wrote Cruickshank, via the NCS’ website. Other Season 1 sports for Piedmont High include volleyball, water polo and football, each given a designation to start in the Orange Tier. But for football an even bleaker announcement came from the CIF, which announced its season must conclude by April 17 in order to have time to complete scheduled for the Fall 2021 football season. “The football season must conclude by April 17, 2021 for the 2021 fall season to commence as scheduled on August 9, 2021,” wrote the North Coast Section in its press release. Piedmont High head coach Jerome Johnson had been hopeful that a season could occur in mid-March, which would allow a schedule of five or six league Photo courtesy of NCS The North Coast Section announced that no official practices are allowed prior to February 1, while the football season must finish by April 17. games. “We’re looking at March… but there are definite worries that we may not have a season,” explained Johnson. The NCS also determined that competition in all sports must be finalized by June 12. For next year (2021-22) Piedmont will likely stay in its current league, the 12 team Western Alameda County Conference. “Luckily we are in a really deep league with a lot of teams, so if stay-at-home orders are lifted, we won’t have any problems getting schedules set. We’d be able to stay within Alameda County,” explained Piedmont’s first-year athletic director Bradley Smet. Perhaps the hardest hit sport is basketball – both girls and boys – which is in the most minimal Yellow Tier, meaning the positivity rate must drop to less than 2 percent. “Basketball has to go a long way to be cleared. Basketball would have to convert to an outdoor sport in order to loosen those guidelines,” explained Smet. articles.text: PHS football coach Jerome Johnson discusses recent headlines with assistant coach Mike Kennedy. It has been a difficult week for deciphering California prep football programs, from big to small. With North Coast Section’s announcement that football must be concluded by April 17, there is a worry by coaches – and sports writers – alike that there might not even be a football season in California. Piedmont High coach Jerome Johnson admitted this week that there is a continued concern in the football community that there won’t be a season. There has been some push for a season starting in mid-March, but a lot has to change in Alameda County and the Bay Area region for that to occur. “There is definitely a cause for worry that we won’t have a season,” Johnson said. “We have some kids who realize this may be the last time they put on a helmet. There is some momentum that we’ll have a season in March, but we have to be as safe as possible. Safety for players and coaches are of the utmost importance.” The CIF and NCS would like football to conclude in the middle of April in order to fit in its Fall 2021 schedule for August. This has led to criticism by some big names in the California prep sports community, including the Los Angeles Times. “Football season is officially over in California, unless the governor and county health officials allow high school teams to play in March by moving sports from orange to red tier,” wrote the Times’ Eric Sondheimer. A bug push has come from the Golden State HS Football Coaches Community, initiated by Serra HS football coach Patrick Walsh. Some 600 coaches from around the state have joined. They are strongly proposing moving football from the Orange Tier classification into the Red. Even then there are many hurdles to be overcome. “I’ve heard a bit about that, and it’s really tough,” explained Piedmont’s Johnson. “We’re going from county to county with health guidelines. If we were to start football tomorrow, our county wouldn’t be able to do it,”. Serra High and the Golden State coalition of coaches are pleading for games based on other states already having competition. “You look at a state I come from, Louisiana, where they are Staff Photo Staff Photo The Piedmont High varsity team in 2019 season. JV coach Daniel King during conditioning in November. playing right now, And you look at us. Our population is so much larger than many of these little counties in the south,” added Johnson, mentioning New Orleans’ population of 390,000 compared to the Bay Area’s 7.7 million. The issues within the state have persuaded some private schools to host their own football games. Orange County schools Capistrano Valley Christian High and Calvary Chapel bypassed the CIF edict and scheduled a full game with referees, uniforms, and all. “Private schools have always followed their own process and have done what they wanted to do, where public schools strictly follow our guidelines,” said Johnson. The CIF promised severe punishment to any program violating health orders, as many coaches spoke out against the two private schools in Southern California. “Any school determined to have participated in or to be conducting interscholastic athletics events in violation of the State’s orders or CIF rules may be subject to CIF Article 22 sanctions including, but not limited to, fines, suspension or dismissal from membership,” wrote the CIF in a press release. “While the CIF understands that the postponement of interscholastic athletics due to the COVID-19 pandemic has had an adverse impact on all of our member schools and student-athletes, the intentional violation of the orders, regulations, and guidance of the Governor’s Office, CDPH, CDE and CIF will not be permitted.” Piedmont High School’s football team has not participated in conditioning since January 1 due to Alameda county’s stay-athome orders. Johnson explained that everyone involved with football would appreciate a firm decision – and some closure to the ongoing agony of indecision. “Everything is politics with their decision. If we’re not going to have football, just say that you won’t have the sport because you’re uncomfortable,” said Johnson. Football still resides in the CIF’s Season 1 of sports for 2021, which includes cross-country, boys’ and girls’ volleyball, and boys’ and girls’ water polo. Only cross-country has been given the green-light once the stay-at-home order is lifted. Football, volleyball, and water polo must reach the Orange Tier. When asked if he expects a firm CIF announcement in the coming weeks, Johnson said it best: “Don’t hold your breath.” Photo by Todd Marshburn

Arrive before mid-morning, especially on Saturdays and holiday weekends,” wrote the park on its website. With park hours limited to 8:00 a.m. to 5 p.m., there is a mad dash to get into the grounds on its two most popular entrances for Bay Area residents: Highway 120 (Big Oak Flat Road) and Highway 140 (El Portal Road). Photo courtesy of CNN The Yosemite Firefall, a magnificent phenomenon when the sun sets perfectly on Horsetail Falls, is about a month away from occurring. Photo courtesy of SF Gate With Yosemite limited to day-use from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., there is a mad dash to get into the park in the morning. Expect 1-3 hour delays if arriving after 9 a.m. Park officials advise visitors to expect two-to-three hour delays if arriving after 9 a.m. Avid hikers who plan ahead can often be spotted waiting to get in as early as 3 a.m. “Expect extremely high visitor concentrations, resulting in extended traffic delays, extremely limited parking, busy trails, and no lodging or campground availability. Expect delays of an hour or more at entrance stations and up to two to three hours in Yosemite Valley. If you are planning to visit Yosemite, plan ahead and arrive early in the morning. You may also experience delays and difficulty finding parking from spring through fall, especially on weekends and around holidays,” wrote Yosemite officials. In order to ease traffic congestion within the park, rangers are asking hikers to leave their car parked for the duration of their day. “Driving from site to site increases traffic congestion and can cause frustration for you and your passengers,” said National Park officials. Yosemite Firefall It will be interesting to see how the National Park handles the annual Yosemite Firefall, expected to take place on February 23-26. The “Firefall” is a rare moment when the setting sun perfectly turns Horsetail Falls to a glowing red ribbon of water flowing down El Capitan. It is anticipated to start around 5:25 p.m. each night and lasts just 15 minutes. They will not be in the old blueprint of the Purple Tier,” said Newsom. This means that North and South Lake Tahoe area can now reopen outdoor dining, wineries, barbershops and salons, and hotels are now eligible to serve tourists after having been limited to serving only essential workers. “This is a huge relief, predominantly for our restaurant industry,” said Truckee council member Dave Polivy, via the SF Chronicle. “This will give people an opportunity, at the very least, to get back to outdoor dining and get some respite from what has been a really overwhelming past six weeks.” Although hotels and lodging is re-opened, amenities like spas and gyms remain closed. articles.text: Photo courtesy of CBS Sports The Warriors pulled off a 115-113 upset of the defending champion Lakers on Monday. They are currently in seventh place of the Western Conference. The Warriors pulled off a mighty upset of the L.A.A Lakers Monday night, 115-113 in comefrom-behind fashion, with help of 26 points from Stephen Curry, including a deep 3-pointer to make it 115-110 with 1:07 remaining. With the game 115-113 and 1.7 seconds left, LeBron James missed the final shot. It improves Golden States’ record to 7-6 and seventh in the Western Conference. The organization is still trying to find its way, but Monday’s win showed some strength. The Dubs are still scoring the 13th most points in the league and have done well to draw fouls, averaging 24.4 per game—5th in the NBA. But their defense and boardwork still needs to improve, even adding C James Wiseman and F Kelly Oubre hasn’t seemed to help; ranking in the bottom-10 for rebounds per game, points allowed, and percentages for allowed field goals and threes, and rebounds per game. They look ahead to the 5th ranked San Antonio Spurs, which are coming off a 125-104 win against the Portland Trail Blazers and walk in as the early favorites.
articles.title: Warriors upset L.A. Lakers

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company’s playwright-in-residence Lauren Gunderson returns with The Catastrophist, a time-jumping tale based on the life and work of virologist Nathan Wolfe, will premiere virtually on January 26, and will be available through February 28. Wolfe, who was named one of Time Magazine’s 100 Most Influential People in the World for his work tracking viral outbreaks, proposed pandemic insurance years before the novel coronavirus outbreak. At the time of his proposal, his views were greeted with disbelief. Now, in a post-COVID world, his story is presented cinematically. “Though not a play about COVID-19, it is a true story of a pandemic expert,” Gunderson explained. “[It is] an interactive deep dive into the profundities Playwright Lauren Gunderson and Nathan Wolfe of scientific exploration and the harrowing realities of facing your own mortality, The Catastrophist is a world premiere theatrical experience built for this moment in time.” The world premiere event is co-produced by Round House Theatre, and will be directed by Jasson Minadakis, Artistic Director of Marin Theatre Company. To order tickets for this virtual play, visit https://www.marintheatre.org/.
articles.title: Marin Theatre Company premieres The Catastrophist on Jan. 26

articles.text: Hao Wu’s “76 Days” The San Francisco Asian Art Museum, in partnership with the Center for Asian American Media (CAAM), is streaming a documentary film that provides a glimpse at the COVID-19 lockdown in Wuhan, China early last year. The film, 76 Days, is available to stream online starting tomorrow, January 21, until Saturday, January 23. The film is an intimate documentary set in the early days of the coronavirus outbreak in Wuhan, the original location of the virus. Filmed deep inside the frontlines of the crisis in four separate hospitals, this award-winning film captures the struggles and resilience of patients and healthcare workers. The title of the documentary references the city’s 76-day lockdown in 2020. The film is deliberately made available tomorrow to mark the one-year anniversary of the start of the Wuhan lockdown. The Asian Art Museum invites patrons to join a discussion with the film’s director Hao Wu, executive producer Naja Pham Lockwood, and director Dr. Jay Xu following tomorrow’s screening. The discussion will be moderated by film producer Claire Aguilar. The first 500 registrants will be sent a link to stream 76 Days online. Members of the Asian Art Museum at all levels will receive complimentary tickets, access to stream the film, and the opportunity to join the panel discussion on Zoom. To obtain tickets, visit https:// calendar.asianart.org/event/76- d ays-a-v it al-look-i nto -t he - covid-19-lockdown-in-wuhan/?- time=1611367200, or log in with your Asian Art Museum membership information. The San Francisco Chamber Orchestra (SFCO) is celebrating Mozart’s birthday with a special digital performance on January 27 that honors the musical icon. The performance, formally named the “Mozart Birthday Celebration Concert,” will feature chamber orchestra all-stars like Liana Berube (violin), Tod Brody (flute), Michael Graham (cello), Keisuke Nakagoshi (piano), and SFCO Music Director Ben Simon (viola), who will perform chamber music by the Salzburg Scribbler. The program includes a Duo for Violin and Viola in G Major, 12 variations on “Ah vous dirai-je, Maman” (“Twinkle” Variations), and Flute Quartet in D Major. Participants are invited to play the orchestra’s Mozart trivia game with Simon, which will be recorded and included in the digital concert on January 27. Email Simon directly at ben@ thesfco.org if you would like to be included in the trivia night. You can join the live stream from the comfort of your home on Wednesday, January 27, or anytime after when the recording will be uploaded on the organization’s website. articles.text: Oakland Symphony presented a virtual inaugural ball on Sunday, January 17, to honor Oakland native and Vice President-elect Kamala Harris. The virtual celebration is now available to view via the symphony’s YouTube channel at https://www.youtube. com/user/oebsym. The program is entitled “Oakland Salutes,” and was curated by Music Director Michael Morgan. It is hosted by Oakland Port Commissioner Michael Colbruno, and includes a message from Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf. “Oakland Salutes” combines a collection of video messages and performances by East Bay musicians and organizations that range in length from less than a minute to nearly seven minutes. Highlights include the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, Oaktown Jazz Workshop, artists from Oakland Ballet Company and the Oakland Asian Cultural Center, the Oakland Interfaith Gospel Chorus, Jazz Mafia, and others. “We are all so proud to have an Oakland, California native as the 49th Vice President,” Morgan said. “The Oakland Symphony has brought together so many members of the Oakland arts community to celebrate this landmark occasion, and we are so excited for people around this country and around the world to learn more about her hometown and its citizens.” Michael Morgan
articles.title: Oakland Symphony salutes Vice President-elect Kamala Harris in virtual inauguration ball

articles.text: Alexander String Quartet will begin 2021 with a virtual concert on Thursday, January 28. The program celebrates the 250th anniversary of Beethoven with a performance of his String Quartet No. 13 in B-flat Major, Op. 130. The Alexander String Quartet (Zakarias Grafilo and Frederick Lifsitz, violin, Paul Yarbrough, viola, and Sandy Wilson, cello) announced their retirement last year, but they continue to perform. They have performed in the major music capitals of the world. The musicians were the first American ensemble to win the London International String Quartet Competition. The quartet has also served as the Ensemble in Residence of San Francisco Performances and have served as Directors of the Morrison Chamber Music Center at San Francisco State University since 1989. The concert is sponsored by Music at Kohl Mansion, longtime friends of the quartet. Alexander String Quartet Tickets are available on https:// musicatkohl.org/buy-tickets/. The performance will begin at 7 p.m. on January 28. The one-hour concert broadcast includes an introduction by musicologist Kai Christiansen, as well as a visit with the musicians.
articles.title: Alexander String Quartet virtual concert on January 28

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will stream its production of La Traviata on Saturday and Sunday, January 30-31. The lavish 2014 performance of Giuseppe Verdi’s La Traviata was the vision of English director John Copley, with staging and choreography by Laurie Feldman. Music Director Nicole Luisotti conducts the orchestra. The opera features soprano Nicole Cabell as Violetta Valery, who delivers a luminous performance of a woman who sacrifices her own happiness in order to save her lover’s family from misery and heartbreak. Richard Tucker Award-winning tenor Stephen Costello is cast as the besotted Alfred Germont, a young man who falls in love with the famous Paris courtesan. The cast also includes Vladimir Stoyanova as Alfredo’s protective father, Giorgio Germont, Daniel Montenegro as Gastone, Dale Travis as Baron Douphol, Hadleigh Adams as Marquis Nicole Cabell and Stephen Costello in San Francisco Opera’s production of La Traviata. d’Obigny, Andrew Craig Brown as Doctor Grenvil and Zanda Svēde as Flora Bervoix. The creative team behind the production includes set designer John Conklin, costume designer David Walker, and lighting designer Gary Marder. La Traviata is performed in Italian with English subtitles and has an approximate running time of two hours and five minutes. The production is available through San Francisco Opera’s “Opera is On” series, a virtual hub for music, backstage stories, and archived performances. Digital content is added throughout shelter-in-place restrictions, and while the opera remains closed to patrons due to the ongoing health crisis. Visit https://sfopera.com/ opera-is-on/streaming/ to obtain tickets for San Francisco Opera’s streaming of La Traviata.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera streaming La Traviata January 30-31

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré Since the release of Shindler’s List, some 170 films have been made about the Holocaust. In the last several months alone, films such as The Reader, The Boy in the Striped Pajamas, and Defiance have screened. Some critics have proffered that Holocaust films have become a genre, rather than stand-alone works that use the Holocaust as a context to ponder greater questions about the human condition. Richard Corliss, of Time magazine, recently pointed out that there are instances in history where far more people were killed than in the Holocaust: the Great Leap Forward in China (close to 30 million), Russia starving the people of Ukraine (10 million). Yet the Holocaust remains the quintessential archetype of evil and an enduring symbol of man’s inhumanity to man. But why? Perhaps, unlike other horrific events that have occurred – more recently in the killing fields of Cambodia, Congo, Darfur and Somalia – Nazi Germany’s Final Solution was, as Corliss points out, deliberate, premeditated and chillingly precise in its plan and execution. Therein, certainly, is the qualitative difference – the overwhelming intentionality. It most likely is why filmmakers and writers have found in the Holocaust a rich cache of material regarding the nature of evil and the inexplicable absence of a defining morality. What better medium than film to explore the darkest parts of the human soul while begging the question as to why it recurs with such predictability. Films about the Holocaust will continue to be made and should be. While Shindler’s List is a work of art, it is also a stark reminder of what occurred while possessing the embedded admonition that we must never forget. The films made about the Holocaust, though open to the criticism of being exploitive and even gratuitous, will always be worth the risk. The film Defiance opens with grainy, documentary-like footage of German soldiers systematically rounding up and executing Jews. These initial scenes quickly set up the tale of the Bielski brothers, Tuvia (Daniel Craig) and Zus (Liev Schreiber), who take refuge in the forests of Belorussia and are soon joined by hundreds of other Jews, desperate to escape the lethal German juggernaut. Eventually, more than 1,200 men, women and children will hide, forming an ad hoc community that is hunted continuously, until finally liberated by the Russians in 1944. At the heart of the film is the dilemma, framed by Friedrich Nietzsche, when he wrote, “If you gaze long into the abyss, the abyss will gaze back into you.” As a revenge-resistance film, had the brothers, and those men who joined them, become a cadre of guerilla fighters waging a war against the Germans, it might have been more satisfying – ambushes, raids and a high German body count. But as a story about a people who struggled with the question of the abyss and yet still prevailed, it is far more interesting. Defiance is a tale that heretofore was likely unknown. Thankfully, the courage of these people, led by Tuvia and Zus Bielski, has now been told and can be added to that archive which asks us to never forget. Defiance. Starring Daniel Craig, Liev Schreiber, Jamie Bell and Alexa Davlos. Directed by Edward Zwick. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated R.

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s latest film, Earwig and the Witch. Movie review by Chris Honoré Earwig and the Witch is a story about a fearless young girl who has grown up in an orphanage nestled in the bucolic English countryside, unaware that her mother had magical powers. Her life changes dramatically when a strange couple takes her in. Puzzled, uncertain, sensing that her new guardians are unusual, she sets about trying to uncover their secrets, and discovers a world of spells and potions and a mysterious song that may be the key to finding the family she always wanted. Earwig and the Witch is the most recent film from Studio Ghibli and was directed by Goro Miyazaki, son of Hayao Miyazaki. It is the Studio’s first CG animated feature and a striking departure from Ghibli’s renown hand-drawn animé. The story is based on the children’s novel of the same name, written by Diana Wynne Jones with a target audience of middle school-age readers. A special note to our readers who have followed the Post’s weekly run of the works of Studio Ghibli and have taken pleasure in the rich animation and wonderful storytelling of Hayao Miyazaki, et al. Earwig and the Witch, while released in Japan in 2020, has thus far only made a trailer available to American audiences, currently shown on HBO MAX. The film is scheduled to open in the U.S. early this year. Hayao Miyazaki is also scheduled to release his latest much anticipated animated feature (handdrawn), How Do We Live, sometime in 2021. articles.text: The 10-year lease agreement between the nonprofit Piedmont Center for the Arts and the City of Piedmont is set to expire this year. The Center aims to renew the lease with the city but has been met with some pushback from two councilmembers and a handful of community members. The city leases a portion of 801 Magnolia Avenue, a former Christian Science Church, to the nonprofit arts group for $1 a year. A proposal to create a cultural arts center was presented to the City Council on March 7, 2011. Council members attending were Mayor Dean Barbieri, and councilmembers Margaret Fujioka, Jeff Wieler, and Garrett Keating. Vice Mayor John Chiang was absent at the meeting. City Administrator Geoff Grote presented a concept of the city-owned property at 801 Magnolia Avenue as a community arts center, as brought to him by a newly formed non-profit group known as the “Piedmont Center for the Arts.” Speaking on behalf of the group was resident Nancy Lehrkind, who noted that 801 Magnolia would be a “perfect venue for smaller performances and other cultural events.” She added that the Piedmont High School theatre was too large and cost prohibitive for smaller groups to use. Grote indicated that the city purchased the property in 2003 from the Christian Science Church formerly located at the site. At the time, it was believed the building would require much rehabilitation before it could be made available for public use. Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) members proposed that they would raise funds from community members to undertake the necessary renovations. After city council direction on March 7, 2011, Public Works Department staff recommended that the lease agreement with the newly formed nonprofit be approved. Public works staff and the Piedmont Fire Department inspected the building for code-compliance, and the PCA secured bids for the necessary repairs and rehabilitation for the building to satisfy the city’s requirements for occupancy. PCA board members were then required, at the request of the council, to submit architectural drawings of sufficient detail and clarity indicating that all the safety, health, and ADA access and occupancy requirements are met. According to city council minutes dated April 18, 2011, “based on staff inspections, the only City-funded repairs necessary to the property may be sewer related. Repair costs could range between $2,500 and $8,000.” The rest of the costly repairs were the responsibility of the PCA. Once the Center was formally approved by council, board members embarked on a successful city-wide fundraising campaign. By the time of the Center’s opening, on August 28, 2011, the PCA had raised approximately $70,000 to transform the space into an inviting cultural arts center for the community. At the council’s meeting on April 18, residents Carole Parker and Steven Nevius, urged council approval of the proposal, emphasizing the value and importance of promoting and providing artistic opportunities to the community. Marion Atherton, Executive Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, spoke in support of the project, stating that it was the Choir’s desire to move its offices back to Piedmont and possibly be a tenant. Councilmember Fujioka was in support of the lease agreement and added that city staff would “need to do its due diligence in making sure that its interests are protected through its lease with the organization.” She indicated her support for the City to determine what work would be necessary to occupy the building. “Piedmonters coming together to meet community needs is a Piedmont tradition,” stated council member Wieler. He reminded members of the council that when the property was purchased by the city, an arts center was one of the concepts discussed for use of this building. Councilmember Keating indicated his conceptual support for the idea. Mayor Barbieri indicated his support to move forward with a report on the condition of the building as a prelude to lease negotiation. Councilmembers approved the first reading unanimously on April 18, with minor modifications, largely based on engineering and construction of the building. The council also stated its preference that the 10-year lease proposal include a clause allowing termination of the lease after seven years upon one year’s written notice, with a repayment to Piedmont Center for the Arts for any unamortized improvements. Grote added that this early termination provision would provide the city with flexibility to pursue different options for this property if so desired. On April 23, 2011 residents in Piedmont received a letter from the Piedmont Center for the Arts announcing themselves as the city’s newest nonprofit group and their intentions for the building at Staff photos Piedmonters flocked to the opening of the Center for the Arts on August 28, 2011, bringing life back to the long-vacant building at 801 Magnolia Avenue. A performance by French horn players Tom Reicher (left) and Stuart Gronnigen of the Berkeley Symphony and Jonathan Ring of the San Francisco Symphony made for a festive ribbon-cutting ceremony. Piedmont Center for the Arts board members Gray Cathrall, Valerie Corvin and Nancy Lehrkind participated in a ceremonial ribbon-cutting on the stage of the Center during the grand opening. 801 Magnolia Avenue. On May 2, 2011, the city council formally approved a lease agreement with PCA for 10 years after second reading approval. Grote explained how the lease agreement with PCA is consistent with the good precedent set by the City approximately 47 years ago related to the development of a community pool at 777 Magnolia Avenue. At that meeting the PCA estimated that it would take approximately eight weeks to complete repairs. Most of the work that needed to be done was cosmetic and included painting, plastering, interior and exterior fixings, and door and window replacements. The center officially opened to the Piedmont community two months later, on August 28, 2011. More than 300 Piedmonters flocked to the center of town for the grand opening of the newly created Center for the Arts, and the long-vacant building was filled to the brim. “The results are spectacular,” commented Mayor Barbieri on opening day. “It is wonderful to see people come together and work so hard and unselfishly to develop a venue that the whole city can enjoy.” “It is amazing how beautifully the facility has transformed into an arts center,” noted Fujioka. Piedmont’s best and brightest attended the opening day, proving that the small town truly had a wealth of artists to draw from. A performance by three symphony French horn players – Tom Reicher and Stuart Gronnigen of the Berkeley Symphony and Jonathan Ring of the San Francisco Symphony – played fanfare music from the top of the stairs, entertaining people as they arrived in time for the ribbon-cutting ceremony. Lining the walls of the two main rooms were bronze sculptures by Bruce Wolfe, who most acknowledge as Piedmont’s “most famous artist.” Abstract paintings by Valerie Corvin, encaustics by Lorna Strotz, and watercolors by Ruth Koch complimented each other on display. Close-up photography by Michelle Hofherr and a geometric piece by architect William Blackwell were included Landscaping was one of the final stages of cosmetic work done to the newly unveiled Piedmont Center for the Arts.

City Administrator Geoff Grote presented a concept of the city-owned property at 801 Magnolia Avenue as a community arts center, as brought to him by a newly formed non-profit group known as the “Piedmont Center for the Arts.” Speaking on behalf of the group was resident Nancy Lehrkind, who noted that 801 Magnolia would be a “perfect venue for smaller performances and other cultural events.” She added that the Piedmont High School theatre was too large and cost prohibitive for smaller groups to use. Grote indicated that the city purchased the property in 2003 from the Christian Science Church formerly located at the site. At the time, it was believed the building would require much rehabilitation before it could be made available for public use. Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) members proposed that they would raise funds from community members to undertake the necessary renovations. After city council direction on March 7, 2011, Public Works Department staff recommended that the lease agreement with the newly formed nonprofit be approved. Public works staff and the Piedmont Fire Department inspected the building for code-compliance, and the PCA secured bids for the necessary repairs and rehabilitation for the building to satisfy the city’s requirements for occupancy. PCA board members were then required, at the request of the council, to submit architectural drawings of sufficient detail and clarity indicating that all the safety, health, and ADA access and occupancy requirements are met. According to city council minutes dated April 18, 2011, “based on staff inspections, the only City-funded repairs necessary Genesis of Piedmont Center for the Arts to the property may be sewer related. Repair costs could range between $2,500 and $8,000.” The rest of the costly repairs were the responsibility of the PCA. Once the Center was formally approved by council, board members embarked on a successful city-wide fundraising campaign. By the time of the Center’s opening, on August 28, 2011, the PCA had raised approximately $70,000 to transform the space into an inviting cultural arts center for the community. At the council’s meeting on April 18, residents Carole Parker and Steven Nevius, urged council approval of the proposal, emphasizing the value and importance of promoting and providing artistic opportunities to the community. Marion Atherton, Executive Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, spoke in support of the project, stating that it was the Choir’s desire to move its offices back to Piedmont and possibly be a tenant. Councilmember Fujioka was in support of the lease agreement and added that city staff would “need to do its due diligence in making sure that its interests are protected through its lease with the organization.” She indicated her support for the City to determine what work would be necessary to occupy the building. “Piedmonters coming together to meet community needs is a Piedmont tradition,” stated council member Wieler. He reminded members of the council that when the property was purchased by the city, an arts center was one of the concepts discussed for use of this building. Councilmember Keating indicated his conceptual support for the idea. Mayor Barbieri indicated his support to move forward with a report on the condition of the building as a prelude to lease negotiation. Councilmembers approved the first reading unanimously on April 18, with minor modifications, largely based on engineering and construction of the building. The council also stated its preference that the 10-year lease proposal include a clause allowing termination of the lease after seven years upon one year’s written notice, with a repayment to Piedmont Center for the Arts for any unamortized improvements. Grote added that this early termination provision would provide the city with flexibility to pursue different options for this property if so desired. A performance by French horn players Tom Reicher (left) and Stuart Gronnigen of the Berkeley Symphony and Jonathan Ring of the San Francisco Symphony made for a festive ribbon-cutting ceremony. Piedmont Center for the Arts board members Gray Cathrall, Valerie Corvin and Nancy Lehrkind participated in a ceremonial ribbon-cutting on the stage of the Center during the grand opening. 801 Magnolia Avenue. On May 2, 2011, the city council formally approved a lease agreement with PCA for 10 years after second reading approval. Grote explained how the lease agreement with PCA is consistent with the good precedent set by the City approximately 47 years ago related to the development of a community pool at 777 Magnolia Avenue. At that meeting the PCA estimated that it would take approximately eight weeks to complete repairs. Most of the work that needed to be done was cosmetic and included painting, plastering, interior and exterior fixings, and door and window replacements. The center officially opened to the Piedmont community two months later, on August 28, 2011. More than 300 Piedmonters flocked to the center of town for the grand opening of the newly created Center for the Arts, and the long-vacant building was filled to the brim. “The results are spectacular,” commented Mayor Barbieri on opening day. “It is wonderful to see people come together and work so hard and unselfishly to develop a venue that the whole city can enjoy.” “It is amazing how beautifully the facility has transformed into an arts center,” noted Fujioka. articles.text: ODC Choreographer Katerina Wong San Francisco’s ODC Dance Commons, located in the Mission District, is co-hosting a virtual premiere of its first production of the year on Friday, January 29. The premiere is co-hosted by ODC and RAWdance, an award-winning contemporary dance company known for transforming theatres and public spaces through a mix of performance and collaboration. The Healer mines the ancient history, systems and beliefs of Traditional Chinese Medicine as a source for physical invention, sensory attunement and solace during trying times. Choreographed by Co-Artistic Director Katerina Wong and created in memory of her aunt, The Healer aims to overcome physical and emotional suffering. The event will include an online preshow class/presentation, a dance premiere filmed at ODC Theater, and a post-show question-and-response forum with artistic collaborators. The full production is approximately one hour. “After months of isolation, anxiety, frustration, loss, grief and uncertainty, we are inspired to offer audiences something more than the concert dance that we had planned to present back in March at the beginning of the first shelter-in-place order,” Wong said. Tickets are available now for all streaming dates. To obtain tickets, visit https://rawdance.org/ events/thehealer/.

articles.text: Guitarist Jaume Torrent of Barcelona, Spain. Paul Harvey, the famous newscaster of yesteryear, once observed that history goes in circles. It’s kind of like an old gas refrigerator. A flame excites gas in a tube. The gas, being excited, is activated, and moves in a predictable course – which happens to be a circle. My news correspondents around the world have sent their personal observations to me. I’d like to relay them to you. The news is contradictory, to say the least. However, have your passport ready and put on your thinking caps. Here we go on a quick trip to the musical capitals of the world. Dateline Usigen, Germany: The birthplace of violinist August Wilhelmj, the person who transformed a beautiful Bach melody into the immortal “Air on the G string.” Music professor Yvonne Smeulers disputes the idea of precise German organization. The city authorities have shut down all musical activity, including the festive celebration of their most important violinist, Wilhelmj. Professor Smeulers puts it into a national perspective. She is Dutch and says that the Dutch are much more open minded than the Germans. She does admit that all of the city’s politicians as well as the important business organizations have worked together to produce a topnotch documentary on the life of their musical hero. Dateline Berlin, Germany: Professor Karen Axelrad informs me that the city government has issued protective masks to all citizens. The government has failed to follow up with guidelines to help the citizens. She tells me that confusion reigns. Dateline Eisenach, Germany: This is the birthplace of the immortal composer Johann Sebastian Bach. Seth Taylor, Concertmaster of the Landeskapelle Orchestra of Eisenach, informs me that all major musical activity has been canceled. He has spearheaded many concerts performed on social media. Seth, an American, was a student of mine when he was in junior high school. A while back he was very disenchanted with the political scene in America. Dateline Barcelona, Spain: Barcelona is a hotbed of coronavirus and political unrest. Our friend and musical colleague Jaume Torrent views the news like a cat watching television…In one ear and out the other. It is his devotion to his art that is supreme. The historic political demonstrations for Catalan independence were outside his apartment. He looked and then returned to his studyand composed some of his most inspired music. In that regard, Torrent is like his hero BeethoPianist Cristiana Pegoraro of Narnia, Italy.
