articles.text: Ben and Cortney Allen with Oakley in front of their tastefully mounted solar power control panels. Recently, after Ben and Cortney Allen moved into their 1905 “forever home”, they installed a 41-panel rooftop solar array with two Tesla storage batteries. “We didn’t set out to be climate activists,” said Ben, CEO of ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) investment specialist Parnassus Investments. “In today’s low-yield investment environment, solar is a pretty good investment.” Ben points out that the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield, hovering around 1%, offers a much lower return than his solar investment, calculated at 5% to 6%. Now the Allens power their home and their personal transportation (via an electric vehicle) with clean electricity generated from their roof. Ben admitted that their family’s electricity bill, which increased under COVID stayat-home orders, got his attention and motivated them to explore solar power quickly. The ability to keep their electricity on during PG&E outages made the decision easier. Ben and Cortney enjoyed working with Power On Solar (www.poweronsolar.com), the professionals who designed and installed their system. Cortney said the team was very communicative and their system has worked flawlessly. They are particularly pleased with Tesla’s well-designed app, which provides real-time information on their power system’s production, usage, and storage. Initially, Cortney thought that the steep roof pitch of their Cape Cod home might be an issue for installation, but it wasn’t. What was a surprise, however, was the number of external boxes and small conduits required to connect the solar panels on the roof of their home and roof of the detached garage. The conduits are connected to the storage batteries mounted inside the garage and to their home’s electrical panel. Cortney worked with the contractors to position the cases and route the conduits inconspicuously to maintain the historic appearance of their home. Ben and Cortney are supportive of Piedmont’s proposed municipal Reach Codes, which the city council is considering to help reduce Piedmont’s greenhouse gas emissions. But the Allens emphasize that other motivations (costs and independence from PG&E) may be more powerful incentives for Piedmont homeowners to invest in reducing their property’s environmental impact. Nevertheless, they concede that regulations are likely necessary to educate homeowners about the speed of change now needed to address climate change, which California is experiencing firsthand with more severe wildfires and more frequent droughts. Asked what advice they might give Piedmonters starting a carbon-neutral odyssey, Ben did not hesitate. “Go vegetarian,” he said. The Allen family is either vegetarian or vegan (with flexibility for a kid who occasionally likes pepperoni and bacon). Ben explained that eating a plant-based diet is the easiest, most beneficial action anyone can take to reduce one’s impact on the planet. “It requires no money, just avoiding one section at the grocery store,” he said. Next, the Allens want to monitor and reduce their water use. To learn more about climate solutions, Cortney and Ben are looking forward to reading Piedmont’s 2021 Readmont selection, This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate, by Naomi Klein. As a regular school library volunteer, Cortney has participated in Readmont nearly every year. This year’s Readmont is funded by a grant from Piedmont Connect (www.piedmontconnect. org). Learn more about the book and the Readmont events planned this year at www.piedmontconnect.org/readmont-2021. Hope Salzer is a member of Piedmont Connect.

articles.text: Rustic Portuguese-Style Potato-Kale Soup with Sausage. Here is a hearty, rustic soup that comes together quickly, is ideal for swapping out ingredients, and perfect for winter. Home cooks have to be flexible these days, preparing dishes based on what’s at hand. This recipe can be the start of many improvisations on its theme. Even a trip to the store doesn’t guarantee they will have everything on the grocery list, and given wait times and lines, most of us are not store-hopping to multiple locations these days to hunt down a specific item. This soup should fly to the top of the list for a warming and satisfying soup when the mood strikes. articles.text: For light, fluffy easy-to bake biscuits, I recommend Cathead Biscuits, as adapted from Cooks Country April/May 2010 edition, Makes 6 very large biscuits INGREDIENTS • 1 1/ 2 cups all-purpose flour • 1 1/ 2 cups cake flour • 1 tablespoon baking powder • 1/ 2 teaspoon baking soda • 1 teaspoon table salt • 8 tablespoons unsalted butter, cut into 1/ 2” pieces and softened • 4 tablespoons pork leaf lard, cut into 1/ 2” pieces (Substitute vegetable shortening if you insist) • 1 1/ 8 cup buttermilk INSTRUCTIONS 1. Adjust an oven rack to upper-middle position and heat oven to 425°F. Butter a 9” round cake pan. 2. Combine flours, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a large bowl. Rub the butter and shortening into flour mixture until it resembles coarse meal. Stir in buttermilk until combined. 3. Use a buttered 1/ 2 cup measuring cup or scoop to transfer 6 heaping portions of dough into prepared pan. Place 5 portions around the perimeter and 1 in the center. 4. Bake until puffed and golden brown, 20 – 25 minutes. Cool in pan for 10 minutes then transfer to a wire rack. Notes: • In a pinch, you can substitute the buttermilk by combining 1-1/8 cups milk with 1 tablespoon lemon juice and letting it sit for about 10 minutes until it thickens slightly. • The dough is fairly moist. Take care to not overmix, as this will result in a denser biscuit. articles.text: Next door to the Piedmont Avenue Library is a building that has been empty for 10 years. Formerly used by the Oakland Unified School District as a Childhood Development Center, it has up to three classroom-sized rooms, bathrooms, a kitchen, and enormous yard areas, with playground equipment, in both front and back. At one side is an abandoned garden plot where children used to grow vegetables. The yard has also been home to a goose, a rabbit and a pet snake. In the 1980s and early 90s, it was alive with activity. Three teachers, each of whom had two or three aides, held classes to prepare young children from low-income families to enter school. The cooks who staffed the kitchen made lunch for the children. Each of Louis Segal’s three children went to the school before they attended Piedmont Avenue Elementary. “It was wonderful, absolutely wonderful,” he said recently. He couldn’t praise it enough and said it helped his family in innuBut when Oakland’s funds for those programs were no longer available, the building was locked and has been empty ever since. There are no funds to restore the Center nor any plans by Oakland School District to do so. articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I am a therapist and am trying to switch to Zoom, Skype or Facetime to meet with my patients. I keep getting freezes and also one of my patients asked me if there are privacy protocols in place for Zoom. Is Zoom, SKYPE and Facetime HIPPA compliant? -Jessica G., Oakland Dear Jessica: Video conferencing, once a tool for only the very tech savvy is becoming the default for doctors, therapists, schools, private teachers, and any professionals who depend on face-to-face experiences with their clients and students. As we all become more comfortable with this tool, questions and challenges are sure to arise. According to market research, 86% of all businesses are using or planning to use video conferencing this year. And for many businesses, employee productivity and relationships with customers is the most important thing. But in medical practices there are different rules restricting the use of video conferencing. HIPAA, or the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, is the law that governs the privacy of patient data. These regulations protect patient health information and determine what can be transmitted on electronic medium. This includes, patient’s name, date of birth, address, email, Social Security number, phone number, health conditions or diagnoses etc. In order for video conferencing software to be HIPAA compliant, it has to be hosted on a compliant server. Microsoft’s consumer Skype product and Apple’s FaceTime are not recommended for medical use, as they are not HIPAA compliant. The free and regular paid versions of Zoom ($14.99/month) are not HIPAA-compliant. Zoom for Healthcare is their only HIPAA compliant product. It’s pretty costly, one user for $200/ month. There are many other health focused video conferencing products, like GoToMeeting ($14/month per organizer) Doxy. me (starting free and $35/month), Simple Practice (which is specifically for therapists, $50/month). These can be costly, but offer lots of features that can be helpful to medical professionals. But there is a huge learning curve for some of them. I know several therapists who do use Zoom, but unless they are using the Healthcare product, their sessions are not HIPAA compliant. Here is a good source for some of the offerings: https:// fitsmallbusiness.com/hipaa-compliant-video-conferencing/ Now to your other issue, video freezes and drop offs. Of course, your signal depends on many things like: 1. Internet speed – are you paying for enough bandwidth? You should be paying for at least 300 MBPS (megabits per second for your download speed) 2. Internet reach – are you close enough to the router? It’s best if you are connected by ethernet cable to your modem/ router. 3. Is anyone else in your house online? I have found that one of my clients solved the drop off problem when she made sure her kids were not playing online video games while she was on a video conference. 4. Is your internet equipment up to date? Some of the older modem/routers cannot handle the higher speeds. Check with your ISP (Internet Service Provider) if you have the latest equipment. We have all had to change the way we do business during the COVID 19 pandemic, but with more communication choices becoming available, our new normal is manageable. articles.text: Residents of The Lake Merritt out for a walk. After the first of the year many of us look at our physical selves and realize that the previous holiday season has resulted in a few extra pounds. This observation often jumpstarts the idea that we need to start exercising. In addition to the holiday gain, living in the COVID-19 world means many of us are staying at home and sitting down more than we usually do. It’s hard for a lot of us to do the sort of exercise we normally enjoy. It’s even harder for people who don’t usually do a lot of physical exercise. It is widely agreed that exercise and physical activity are important as we age. Staying active can help us remain independent by preventing loss of physical mobility. Besides keeping your body healthy, research has shown that physical activity also helps the brain and may slow age-related cognitive decline. We’ve heard it all before, but it bears repeating. The World Health Organization, and many others tell us that “regular physical activity benefits both the body and mind. It can reduce high blood pressure, help manage weight and reduce the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and various cancers - all conditions that can increase susceptibility to COVID-19.” Regular, moderate-intensity exercise has immune-boosting benefits that may help your body fight off infections and many viruses. How can we start? Walking is a great way for older adults to exercise. Frequent walking can build endurance helping each of us walk farther, faster, or even uphill with greater ease. The pandemic has also made it very difficult to exercise in other ways we have become accustomed to. With gyms closed, many exercise classes are unavailable. Yet, virtual fitness classes have sprung up online. These allow you to interact with other people in a fun way, which may be just the motivation we need to keep up with our fitness regime. Program Director Ryan Wilcox has set up The Lake Merritt’s exercise program online through Zoom. This allows residents to exercise in their own apartment, or join the group where they can exercise in a way that is socially distanced while wearing masks. Regular physical activity is essential for everyone under normal circumstances. It is especially important during the COVID-19 Pandemic. Although many things feel beyond our control right now, we do have the ability to be creative and to build physical activity and exercise into each of our days. We may even look back on this difficult time as the turning point when we learned new ways to build our physical health and resilience. articles.text: Piedmont resident, Pres. of Wheaton and Wellesley Colleges, a lifelong champion of equal rights Dale Rogers Marshall, a resident of Piedmont starting in 1970, died from complications of COVID on January 14, 2021. A political scientist and academic administrator dedicated to equal opportunity for all, Dr. Marshall was 83. As president of Wheaton College in Norton, Massachusetts, from 1992-2004, Dr. Marshall oversaw the Campaign for Wheaton, a $90 million fund supporting student scholarships and academic inclusiveness. At Wheaton, Dr. Marshall pushed to find and hire academics from under-represented groups, as she had at Wellesley College where she was Dean of the College from 1986-1992 and Acting President from 1987-1988, and at UC Davis before that as Associate Dean in the College of Letters and Science. A much larger amount of data was just released from North Carolina where 90,000 students and 10,000 teachers went back to school when COVID case rates were up to four times higher than our “purple tier” here in California. Nevertheless, there were only 32 school-based transmissions between September and November. These are tiny, incredibly reassuring numbers. The North Carolina schools are not well-resourced private schools, but public schools, where half of the students are students of color. The success is not based on intensive resource investments, but rather on wearing masks and social distancing. It’s also important to note that the limited outbreaks in these schools were not among middle or high school students, but pre-k and special needs children. LC: So, is it safe to open now, even while we are in the purple tier? JN: Yes. The state has already allowed open schools to stay open during our stay-at-home orders. And under the newest guidelines, all K through 6 schools can open when the daily case rate is below 25 per 100,000. This means that all elementary schools have permission to open very soon, likely by February 1. But the tragedy with these new guidelines is that 7 through 12 graders are completely left out, awaiting return to the red tier before their schools can open. LC: Let’s talk about middle and high school students. We mostly only hear about plans to bring back elementary school kids. I heard you say on a panel this week that they should go back to in-person learning, too. JN: Absolutely. Our adolescents are developmentally driven to be increasing those important social and emotional connections outside of the family. They are particularly hard-hit by these closures. No one has ever characterized adolescence as an easy time in life, and California’s policy of school closures has made it considerably harder. Even though transmission rates are higher among adolescents than younger children, data shows that high schools can operate safely, and therefore, they should be allowed to do so. LC: To open schools now, and safely, what precautions need to be in place? JN: Masks and social distancing, which together, block about 90 percent of transmissions – on par with vaccines. In addition, schools need to be symptom screening, and classroom doors need to be kept open to increase airflow. LC: Many schools are making plans to reopen, but it’s a hybrid model versus an all-day in-person. Is a hybrid model safer? JN: No, not necessarily. The bulk of evidence no longer supports the theory that fewer school hours means less COVID transmission. Students are more closely supervised at school than during remote learning. So reduced school often translates to more time in higher risk environments. LC: Do we need to wait until all teachers are vaccinated, and what about until students are vaccinated? JN: No, studies have already shown that schools can be operated safely, because masks and distancing block transmission. Data from Marin, North Carolina, and elsewhere demonstrate that we can keep both teachers and students safe, even before vaccines. LC: Is it safe though to open schools, even with this new strain? We keep hearing that it is more contagious. JN: Yes, it is safe, even when the new variant becomes dominant here, which could be as soon as March. The likelihood of getting COVID when you’re exposed is 11 percent. New contact tracing data from the UK shows that transmissability has increased to 14.7 percent with the new variant. Although that 11 to 14.7 percent change represents a large relative increase, it’s an absolute increase of only 3.7 percent, which does not fundamentally change whether schools can operate safely. LC: You said on a panel discussion that if you knew now what you knew in March, you would have never recommended closing schools as a safety precaution. Why is that? JN: We closed schools in March because we thought that children would be the primary drivers of COVID, like they are for the flu. Now we know that we were wrong. Kids are less likely to get COVID and transmit COVID than adults. Of the more than 30,000 COVID deaths in California, there have been only six deaths among people under age 15. If we had these numbers back in March, we never would have closed our schools. LC: If we know that schools can open now and open safely, and we know what to do to keep kids and teachers safe, why aren’t schools reopening? JN: The reason the Bay Area is living through the longest school closures on the planet is mired in politics. The California Teacher’s Association is one of the most powerful unions in the country, and has provided key support to Gavin Newsom. If the CTA does not want to open schools, Gavin Newsom is not going to mandate reopening. We need to get the safety data to union leaders so that we can move forward in a climate of trust and meet as many of their needs as quickly as possible, so that all of our kids, regardless of income, can be back in school by February. Our children have a right to in-person education, and we know how to do this. It’s time to get moving.

articles.text: This letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: It is my pleasure to write in support of the Piedmont Center of the Arts and the renewal of their lease with the City. Having performed, presented, and attended performances at the PCA, I can say with emphatic certainty that it is a cultural gem in the heart of Piedmont, and I urge you to give them every consideration in this matter. It became clear to me that this venue was at the level of the music, and I tucked that experience away in my memory. One year later I launched the San Francisco International Piano Festival with support from Piedmont Community members Craig and Letitia Casebeer. Soldout crowds, open air atmosphere, visual art, and world class piano playing in a warm and approachable environment. I have performed at the PCA myself on a number of occasions and have always found it to be a gratifying experience.
